title: Experimental Evidence on Structural State Dependence in Demand
abstract: The paper provides nonparametric estimates of structural state dependence from a natural field experiment for 223 brands.

title: Frontiers: Reducing Disparity Between LLMs and Humans: Optimal LLM Sample Calibration
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to measure human preferences and opinions, but their outputs can diverge from human responses. We introduce human mimicry calibration (HuMCal), a post hoc, model-agnostic method that uses aggregate human benchmark data to learn how to combine LLM outputs from different prompts, personas, and model checkpoints. In applications to consumer transaction data and public opinion surveys, HuMCal improves agreement with human benchmarks over standard aggregation rules, and the calibrated weights often remain useful across time, geography, industry, and question clusters.

title: Injunctive Norms Outperform Reciprocity: Tip Request Messages Can Increase Tipping Without Reducing Demand
abstract: Tip request messages are marketing communications that can help digital platforms balance customer spending with worker effort and compensation. We report the first field experiments testing how three appeals based on tipping motivations—injunctive norms (“It’s customary to leave a tip for the seller’s service”), personalized reciprocity, and impersonal reciprocity—affect tipping and future demand in a global freelance marketplace. Overall, the norms message increased tipping the most, and did so without reducing returning demand, showing that tip request messages can motivate customer tipping to better incentivize and compensate gig workers.

title: The Problem of Ignoring the Ignorability Assumption in Advertising Measurement: A Matrix Completion Solution
abstract: This paper frames the overlap violation problem in online advertising auctions as a missing-data problem and proposes a matrix completion approach to correct the resulting bias in observational studies with algorithmic ad allocation.

title: Collective Sensemaking When Purchasing Complex B2B Services: How Buying Centers Construct and Align Interpretations of Vendor Service Offering
abstract: Buying centers evaluate complex B2B service offerings not by aggregating independent assessments but through collective interpretive processes that buying center theory has documented structurally without explaining. This study introduces collective service offering sensemaking as a theoretical lens that explains how buying centers construct, contest, and align interpretations of a vendor’s service offering. Drawing on a multi-phase qualitative multiple-case study of six organizations (24 interviews, 3 focus groups, 5 procurement-meeting observations; 2022–2024), we show that service evaluations originate in identity-rooted interpretive frames that differ across technical, financial, procurement, and operational roles. Through interpretive bridging, narrative negotiation, controlled dissent, and evaluative rituals, buying centers transform fragmented meaning structures into interpretive sufficiency, a threshold that enables collective action despite persistent misalignment. The central contribution is interpretive sufficiency: buying centers act on negotiated adequacy rather than consensus, convergence, or shared understanding, through three forms of service value alignment. Three supporting elements explain how the threshold is reached: identity-rooted frames generate the divergence, four interactional mechanisms convert it into workable evaluations, and contextual anchors condition which interpretations gain authority. These elements are not unique to services; what changes under service conditions is their function, salience, and intensity once value-in-use cannot be verified before adoption.

title: EXPRESS: THE SOUND OF WORDS: VERBAL AND VOCAL CUES IN CUSTOMER SATISFACTION
abstract: Technology-mediated service interactions, such as phone calls, generate rich behavioral signals that firms currently struggle to monitor in real time. Post-interaction surveys provide delayed and unrepresentative feedback, leaving satisfaction invisible as calls unfold. Satisfaction judgments depend on how evaluative meaning is communicated across two channels, verbal content and vocal delivery, whose relative contribution varies by outcome type. The authors analyze 1,144 real-world service calls, each coded as dissatisfied, neutral, or satisfied, using text-only, audio-only, and multimodal deep learning models. Dissatisfied calls are identified from transcripts alone as accurately as by multimodal models, since customers articulate problems and remedy expectations explicitly. Neutral and satisfied calls depend more strongly on vocal interpretation, and cross-attention models outperform text-only alternatives precisely where verbal content is absent or insufficiently distinctive to separate outcomes. The findings identify a boundary condition on interactivity, whereby vocal cues add predictive value when evaluative meaning is absent or insufficiently distinctive between outcomes, not when it is explicit and clearly distinguishes outcomes, as is the case for dissatisfied calls.

title: The Sound of Good Service: How Dominant and Submissive Language in AI Voice Assistants Shapes Consumer Responses Across Service Settings
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) voice assistants (VAs) function as service agents, delivering information and recommendations tailored to users’ specific needs. VA agents can engage in voice conversations, in which they may convey dominance or submissiveness in response to consumer requests, thereby shaping consumer experiences across service settings. Drawing on the notion of master–servant relationships from assemblage theory, this research examines how, and in which contexts, VAs should use dominant and submissive language to shape consumer interactions. Across six experimental studies, we find that VAs’ submissive language increases usage intentions and perceived interaction value by enhancing rapport and, in turn, comfort, which ultimately drives these consumer responses, even in authority-oriented service settings. However, under time pressure, VAs’ use of either dominant or submissive language equally predicts rapport, thereby disrupting the serial pathway through comfort that leads to usage intentions and perceived interaction value. Together, these findings help specify how service managers can best design VA language to enhance the value of consumer interactions with this technology in service contexts.

title: Agentic AI Personalization in Advertising: Realizing the True Potential of N = 1
abstract: With the rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (AI), we have come closer than ever to achieving the holy grail of personalizing advertisements to individual consumers, i.e., the ideal of N = 1. AI-driven ad serving platforms act with unprecedented agency, dynamically creating highly tailored appeals and experiences. Such “agentic AI personalization” has both positive and negative consequences. This article traces the evolution from analog personalization to agentic personalization. It then explicates the latter concept in terms of breadth, depth, and length of personalized messaging. It overviews the processes underlying agentic AI personalization and describes the dualities inherent in both its foundation and operation. Finally, it offers a theoretical framework for studying the effects of agentic AI personalization on consumer responses to advertisements, followed by an illustrative set of propositions for empirical testing.

title: The Role of Institutions in the Relationship Between Informal Competition and New Product Development in Emerging Economies
abstract: ABSTRACT Academic Summary Research has argued that informal competition (IC)—the competitive pressure from firms that are unregistered but derive income from the production of legal goods and services—increases formal (i.e., legally registered) firms' engagement in new product development (NPD) in emerging economies. However, other studies have suggested that IC may decrease such engagement. Drawing on an institutional perspective, we argue that the relationship between IC and NPD is contingent on the level of IC and the influence of formal and informal institutions. A multilevel analysis of 29,520 formal firms across 21 emerging economies indicates an inverted U‐shaped relationship between IC and NPD probability. Low to moderate levels of IC increase NPD probability, whereas higher levels reduce it. The findings also reveal that this relationship varies across emerging economies, with significant cross‐level interactions between IC and elements of formal (e.g., regulatory control, availability of finance) and informal institutions (e.g., survival vs. self‐expression and traditional vs. secular‐rational values) shaping NPD probability. Managerial Summary Informal competition can stimulate formal firms' new product development at low to moderate levels, but high levels of IC can discourage it. Because informal firms spur innovation among their formal counterparts, policymakers should not automatically seek to eliminate IC. Instead, they should consider IC as a changing condition and adapt enforcement to its intensity. At low to moderate levels of IC, minimal enforcement may be appropriate as the innovation and consumer benefits associated with IC may outweigh its costs. As IC becomes more intense and begins to undermine formal firms' NPD, policymakers can tighten enforcement while offering informal firms incentives to formalize. For managers, the findings suggest that the strategic response to IC should also depend on its intensity. When IC is low, formal firms may continue to innovate despite financial constraints; managers can therefore pursue low‐risk, affordable products using frugal innovation methods, while policymakers can support these efforts through improved access to finance. Managers are also well‐advised to consider the institutional context. Unlike their counterparts in countries leaning toward survival values (e.g., India), formal firms operating in societies that lean toward self‐expression values (e.g., Uruguay) are more likely to engage in NPD when IC is low; the probability decreases as IC becomes higher.

title: Color me aroused while keeping the cool
journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
abstract: Abstract Drawing on visual complexity theory and the arousal properties of color, this paper challenges the prevailing assumption that only warm (longer wavelength) or highly saturated colors can induce arousal in consumers. Instead, we propose a novel pathway: multicolor logos with cool hues can elicit arousal through triggering curiosity. Across a total of eight experiments (seven preregistered with a total of 1,724 participants recruited), of which six experiments are reported in the main text, including a behavioral lab study employing biometric measures (eye tracking, galvanic skin response, pupil dilation), and three studies utilizing real product choices, we consistently find that multicolor cool logos are more arousing than single cool color designs. This heightened, curiosity-driven arousal subsequently impacts marketing outcomes, including willingness to pay and choice. These findings offer marketers alternative strategies for inducing arousal in brand communications and provide actionable guidelines for effectively designing logos.

title: Spoiler alert! Watch movies before they are spoiled
journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: Machine Learning Instrument Variables for Causal Inference
abstract: A machine learning framework for constructing strong instrumental variables from weak exogenous data achieves semiparametric efficiency with applications to advertising and demand estimation.

title: EXPRESS: Incentive Design for Sales Managers: Impact on Resource Allocation and Performance
abstract: Many firms struggle to design effective incentives for sales managers . Yet despite a vast literature on salespeople’s incentives, little theoretical or empirical research has examined managers’ incentive structures. The authors address a common dilemma that firms face: Should managers’ incentives be based on achieving an aggregate target ( Aggregate Target Scheme , ATS) or instead be linked to the target achievement of each individual territory or salesperson ( Individual Target Scheme , ITS)? A quasi-experiment reveals that, despite ATS’s flexibility and apparent alignment with firm objectives, an ATS-to-ITS transition improved performance , with larger gains among lower-performing and higher-span territories. A scenario-based experiment with sales managers suggests that these effects may stem from the reallocation of resources from high to low performers but provides no evidence of an increase in managers’ overall resource investment. A survey of sales leaders indicates that a sales star bias —a managerial tendency to overallocate resources toward high performers relative to their marginal returns—likely drives suboptimal resource allocation under the flexible ATS. Finally, a supplementary field study documents that, following an ATS-to-ITS transition, managers increased joint fieldwork , especially with the lowest performers, and performance again improved. These results provide insights into managerial incentive design and offer guidance for firms.

title: Common ownership and consumer welfare
journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
abstract: Abstract Rival firms with shared institutional investors (i.e., common owners) may compete less aggressively, potentially harming consumer welfare. Yet, research on common ownership has primarily focused on firm performance, often overlooking welfare outcomes or revealing contradictory results. This paper adopts a strategic network perspective to examine how common ownership affects firms’ service quality and pricing levels, which directly impact consumer welfare, and how customer and competitor factors that alter the focus of competitive strategy moderate these effects. To test the hypotheses, the authors analyze a rich, multi-market dataset of U.S. airline firms from 1995 to 2025. Findings reveal that competing firms with higher common ownership tend to have lower service quality and set higher prices. However, this effect is attenuated for firms with high customer-asset value and amplified among rivals competing across multiple markets. The findings demonstrate common ownership’s influence on firms’ marketing mix strategies and offer actionable insights for managers, policymakers, and investors.

title: Managing the dual nature of customer engagement in product innovation: A sensegiving and sensemaking perspective
journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: EXPRESS: Interactive Blind Lead-In Ads and Purchase Conversion: The Roles of Completion and Creative Design Features
abstract: Interactive display advertising increasingly employs delayed product disclosure in multi-stage formats, yet little is known about how they affect purchase behavior when exposure to the reveal depends on users’ interaction. This article studies interactive blind lead-in (BLI) ads with a randomized field experiment: over 109,000 customers of a book retailer were assigned to a BLI ad with delayed reveal or a static ad with immediate disclosure. The experiment identifies a boundary condition on the transfer of prior interactivity findings to user-controlled delayed-reveal advertising: assignment to the BLI format does not increase average purchase conversion, as interactivity’s positive mechanisms need not produce a conversion gain when most exposures end before the reveal. Using random assignment as an instrument, completing the BLI sequence increases long-term purchase conversion among compliers (a 46.6% lift; 437 completions per incremental purchase), indicating that delayed-reveal interactivity is effective only when users meaningfully interact with the ad. Completion varies across ads consistent with a Cost-of-Progress framework: early informational cues predict higher completion, late-stage textual and visual complexity predicts lower completion, and social cues predict higher completion when placed before the final stage. A supplementary study shows that the downstream impact of BLI interaction depends on overall hedonic experience.

title: EXPRESS: The Dark Side of Competition for Market Share: Competitive Pressure May Trigger Corporate Misconduct
abstract: There is an ongoing debate about the role of market share and market share–based competition in shaping corporate behavior and performance. This study advances the discussion by analyzing how a firm’s specific competitive situation drives corporate misconduct and how such misconduct affects future market share. Based on a theory-in-use approach, the authors propose the Theory of Market Share–Based Competitive Pressure (TMCP) and introduce four new market share–based constructs that reflect different dimensions of competitive pressure. Using a global sample of 2,145 firms across 254 industries over 11 years, they find that firms that are closer to market leadership and more closely followed by competitors are more prone to misconduct. The results demonstrate that misconduct systematically weakens the very market positions that created the pressure in the first place, with particularly strong penalties for environmental and governance–related misconduct incidents. Importantly, organizational characteristics such as compensation design, board composition, and marketing capabilities condition the extent to which competition translates into corporate misconduct. Together, these findings demonstrate that while misconduct may appear as a shortcut to defend competitive positions, it ultimately undermines them, and there are ways to reduce incentives for misconduct in the first place.

title: The Effects of Search Interface on Consumer Preferences: Evidence from a Randomized Experiment
abstract: While structured search interfaces—such as filters and sorting tools—help consumers reduce search frictions on digital platforms, they also shape how consumers encounter product information during search. This paper studies how search interface design influences revealed preferences and market outcomes. We develop a theoretical framework linking interface design to attribute preferences through salience reallocation and information-based preference updating. The framework generates two predictions that can be formally derived: restricting faceted filters reduces the concentration of attribute importance weights (i.e., preference dispersion) and increases the diversity of products chosen (i.e., choice diversity). We test these predictions using a randomized, incentive-aligned online experiment in which 1,200 participants searched for wireless headphones on a custom-built e-commerce platform. Restricting filters led consumers to explore more broadly and resulted in more evenly distributed attribute importance weights and more diverse, higher-priced product choices. Mediation analysis further suggests that increased exploration was associated with shifts in attribute preferences. Our findings demonstrate that search interface design can construct, rather than merely reveal, consumer preferences.

title: Return on AI (RoAI): A framework for assessing AI investments in the marketing organization
journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping marketing as firms increasingly delegate activities and decisions previously performed by marketers to AI systems. As AI assumes a greater role in market-facing decisions, understanding the value firms realize from these investments becomes increasingly important. Building on marketing accountability and resource-based theory, we develop a Return on AI (RoAI) framework that conceptualizes AI investment through the people, processes, and capabilities that enable its deployment and governance. RoAI evaluates incremental benefit while accounting for value retention, evidence durability, and the full costs of deployment over time. The framework identifies a distinctive consequence of delegated judgment, wherein AI can improve current performance while reducing the experiential practice through which marketers develop and maintain the judgment required to evaluate and redirect the AI solution. This mechanism helps explain heterogeneity in AI returns across firms and over time. We develop seven testable predictions and an agenda for research on creating, appropriating, and sustaining value from AI.

title: Identifying and managing milestones in consumers’ goal journeys
journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
abstract: Abstract Understanding consumers’ holistic journeys as unfolding events is paramount for managing service design and delivery. Touchpoints, “moments of truth” and critical incident research primarily focus on firm-facing events and consumers’ evaluations of firm encounters, rather than critical events in consumers’ own goal pursuit. This article introduces and uncovers the significance of milestone events in consumers’ journeys. Milestones are significant events that mark a major step or turning point in a consumer’s journey. Multi-stage, multi-context qualitative consumer journey research is used to inductively identify the key features and implications of milestones. They are distinct from other service events and consequential for consumers’ lives. This research fills a significant research gap in understanding consumer goal journeys. Identifying and understanding consumers’ milestone events enables service firms to support and improve goal progression; increase confidence in success; help consumers prepare for and interpret milestone outcomes; and manage risk by adjusting or pivoting from the goal.

title: De-Sludging High-Friction Frontlines: Designing an AI-Mediated Service Gateway for Mental Health
abstract: Nearly one billion people suffer from mental disorders globally, yet 35 to 85 percent receive no treatment even when services are available, affordable, and known to them. This paradox suggests that the primary barrier to utilization is not only structural supply failure but also behavioral friction at the mental health service entry threshold. Drawing on sludge theory and administrative burden research, we conceptualize these barriers as service sludge—cognitive, emotional, and process frictions preventing vulnerable consumers from crossing the threshold. We adopt a design science research methodology and design MyMatcher, an AI-mediated service gateway—a pre-encounter frontline entity comprising three modules: a sensing engine that infers clinical intent from vernacular distress language, a low automated social presence (ASP) chatbot designed to reduce the social risk of disclosure, and a provider-matching module that collapses provider search into a curated shortlist. Through diagnostic and evaluative interviews with mental health practitioners, complemented by classification validation on a labeled corpus of over 4,000 texts, we derive three design principles and three research propositions for de-sludging high-friction service frontlines. Theoretically, we extend the 3A (Affordability, Access, and Awareness) framework by introducing Agency as a fourth behavioral dimension; we introduce the service gateway as a pre-encounter entity distinct from augmentation and substitution models; and we theorize an inversion of intimacy, the proposition that lower ASP facilitates sensitive disclosure in stigma-laden contexts, which qualifies a central assumption in service technology research. The framework is designed to generalize beyond mental health to high-stigma, high-complexity domains where behavioral frictions prevent consumers from acting on structural access to relevant services.

title: Synthetic diversity: Racial depictions influence consumer responses to AI ‐generated models in advertising
abstract: Abstract As brands seek to increase racial representation in their advertising, many are turning to AI‐generated images of humans (i.e., synthetic models) as a scalable solution. This research demonstrates that consumer reactions to synthetic models are asymmetric, depending on the racial identity being depicted. Across five studies, we demonstrate that disclosing the AI‐generated nature of models lowers firm evaluations when the featured models are from racially underrepresented groups (e.g., Black, Hispanic, and Asian models), but not when they are White. This effect is driven by reduced perceptions of the authenticity of the firm's inclusion efforts, which in turn elevate inferences of manipulative intent. Importantly, these negative effects can be mitigated when consumers are informed that the firm is owned by members of the depicted racial community, suggesting that credible signals of authentic community ties can neutralize the evaluative penalty of AI disclosure. Our findings extend research on racialized depictions in advertising by identifying synthetic depiction as a novel threat to the evaluative benefits of minority representation, and by theorizing why this threat operates asymmetrically by race. More broadly, our results highlight that technological innovations in advertising cannot be divorced from the social and historical contexts that shape their meaning.

title: The Fragile Encounter: Service Interaction Vulnerability in Emergency Department Care
abstract: This paper investigates service interaction vulnerability (SIV) within emergency departments, where both patients and providers are susceptible to heightened vulnerability. Providers face exhaustion from long shifts, high patient volumes, challenging patient behaviors, and systemic constraints contributing to emotional exhaustion. Patients, meanwhile, feel vulnerable due to illness or injury and their dependency on providers, compounded by the ways in which presenting certain characteristics, such as intimate partner violence, substance use, or suicidal ideation, can shape how they are perceived and treated in the system. These dynamics often result in unintended negative consequences that exacerbate perceived vulnerability for both patients and providers. Employing a mixed-method approach, including hospital data analysis and netnography, this study introduces a theoretical framework for SIV that illuminates how patient–provider interactions can exacerbate or mitigate vulnerabilities. By examining how these interactions shape the likelihood of service failure or successful service encounters, the study advances understanding of dual vulnerability in high-stakes service contexts.

title: AI in Disguise—Quasi-Experimental Analysis of a Large-Scale Deployment of AI-Generated Ads
abstract: As Taboola prepared to launch its GenAI Ad Maker, a tool that lets advertisers create ad images within the platform, it faced a consequential question about whether AI-generated ad images would perform well with real consumers, and under what conditions. Working with Taboola, we construct a quasi-experimental comparison of 4,633 ‘sibling ads,’ meaning AI-generated and human-made images launched by the same advertisers, in identical campaign settings, at the same time. These ads span more than 369 million impressions and 2.5 million clicks. We do not find a detectable average click-through-rate disadvantage for AI-generated images relative to their human-made siblings. However, this average masks an important boundary condition: ads with AI-generated images outperform human-made ads when the AI images do not ‘look like AI.’ We identify key visual features influencing consumers’ perceptions of whether an ad looks AI-generated. While AI generates sharper, clearer, and less blurry images with larger faces, consumers associate these features with human-made ads. On the other hand, in line with consumers’ expectations, aesthetics, lower warmth, and intense color saturation in ads signal AI generation. These findings support Taboola’s roll-out communication, advertiser guidance, and continued refinement of the GenAI Ad Maker.

title: The Motivational Paradox: How Aspirational-Goal Communications Influence Sales Performance and Information Acquisition
abstract: This study examines how aspirational-goal communications influence sales agents’ performance and information-seeking behavior. In a field experiment across 100 stores in Sweden, agents in the treatment group received daily personalized text messages with aspirational sales goals tailored to their prior performance. Results show that these communications increase sales performance, particularly among low-performing agents, primarily through higher unit sales. At the same time, they reduce agents’ willingness to monitor within-day sales progress—reflecting the ostrich effect—which can adversely affect performance. Information acquisition, in the form of sales-progress monitoring, typically aids effort provision, but aspirational-goal communications suppress such behavior, complicating performance management. These findings highlight the dual effects of aspirational-goal communications: while they enhance motivation, they may also prompt information avoidance. The study contributes to research on goal setting and sales management by clarifying the trade-offs in designing effective motivational and communication strategies.

title: EXPRESS: Expanding Markets or Capturing Share? The Competitive Effects of Subscriptions on Spending in Restaurant Delivery
abstract: Subscription programs are increasingly central to platform strategy, but their effects on competitors and category demand remain unclear. The authors study restaurant delivery subscriptions using individual-level transaction data on Postmates Unlimited, the first widely available U.S. subscription program in the category, and DoorDash's later DashPass program. Using a matched, staggered difference-in-differences design, they find that signing up for Postmates Unlimited is associated with a 90.4% increase in spending at the focal firm, with no significant average change in competing-firm spending and no offsetting decline in adjacent food categories, consistent with category expansion. Competitive effects depend on customers' prior platform usage. For “singlehomers” (who only used Postmates prior to subscribing), subscribing is associated with increased spending at both the focal firm and competing platforms, even after cancellation. For “multihomers” (who had also previously used competing platforms), the focal-firm effect is larger, and competing-firm spending falls while customers remain subscribed; after cancellation, the focal-firm lift persists, but the decrease in competitor spending does not. DashPass results are broadly similar, but customers with prior Postmates subscription experience show little increase in category spending. Together, these findings suggest subscriptions can both expand markets and capture share, depending on prior platform usage and subscription experience.

title: Perceived-Control Salience in Service Recovery: Area-Level Economic Disadvantage and Consumer Disputes
abstract: This study develops a perceived-control salience framework for understanding the experiences of consumers in economically disadvantaged areas during service recovery. Drawing on 141,251 complaint narratives submitted to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, we examine how seven salience dimensions relate to dispute escalation. The results suggest that cognitive-control and behavioral-control salience have the strongest positive associations with disputing. Emotional-control salience, decision-control salience, and predictive-control salience have weaker positive associations, whereas information-control salience is negatively associated with dispute escalation. The study contributes to service recovery and consumer vulnerability research by showing how economic disadvantage changes which control-related cues become behaviorally predictive in institutional complaint systems. The findings suggest that effective recovery should reduce comprehension burdens, lower action costs, and avoid treating disclosure alone as sufficient consumer support.

title: Pet-owner synchrony: Operationalization, application, and implications
journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
abstract: Abstract Despite the pet industry’s significant economic and social importance, academic attention to this sector of the economy has been limited. Rather than focusing solely on the household demographics of pet ownership or the attitudinal components of the pet-owner relationship, we explore actual purchase decisions of pet owners. In this study, we examine pet-owner synchrony, a behavioral operationalization of pet-owner relationships that is grounded in attachment theory, anthropomorphism, and the extended self. Utilizing scanner data from 875,853 market baskets including 23 million transactions collected from a regional supermarket chain, we analyze cross-category co-occurrence patterns within shopping baskets. Our analysis reveals affinities, or parallels, in pet owners’ purchases of health and wellness products and hedonic products for both themselves and their pets, which we attribute to pet-owner synchrony. We identify two moderators that influence the strength of pet-owner synchrony: pet type (cat versus dog) and the presence of young children in the household. In addition, we evaluate how basket size, holidays, and price elasticities impact pet-owner synchrony. Our findings deliver useful insights into pet-owner relationships, have direct implications for retail and manufacturing managers, and yield recommendations for public policy.

title: Marketing misinformation in the age of AI
abstract: Abstract We shine a spotlight on marketing misinformation—claims about products and brands that contradict or distort verifiable facts. Misinformation may be created unintentionally or intentionally by companies, competitors, customers, or third parties seeking to harm companies or consumers. We focus on the role of AI in creating, obfuscating, and disseminating misinformation in the form of text, audio, images, and videos generated using large language models. This type of information can pose a substantial risk for brand safety. Consumers may be aware that AI can generate misinformation but may lack the ability to guard against it. We discuss how different stakeholders in the information ecosystem can help in the prevention and correction of misinformation and propose a future research agenda in this critical and fast‐growing area.

title: The ripple effects of customer orientation: Personal, vicarious, and temporal pathways to frontline employee well-being
journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: EXPRESS: Correcting omitted-variable bias without instruments: An ICA-based alternative to Gaussian copula methods
abstract: This paper proposes an instrument-free correction for omitted-variable bias and overcomes a key limitation of Gaussian copula control function (GCCF) approaches. Omitted-variable bias is the most common source of endogeneity in marketing, and many articles apply GCCF to address it. Yet GCCF require a nonlinear regressor-error relation, whereas textbooks assume linear, additive relationships between regressors and omitted variables. The authors prove that GCCF is biased in classical omitted-variable settings. Extant articles that address omitted-variables with GCCF also show language cues implicitly assuming linear relationships, which invalidate the use of GCCF. The proposed endogeneity correction is tailored to this prominent case, utilizing independent component analysis (ICA). It assumes a latent normally distributed component that additively influences both the endogenous regressor and the error. This can be interpreted as the sum of omitted variables, which, according to the Central Limit Theorem, add up to a normal distribution. Through ICA, this component is identified and extracted from the endogenous regressor, rendering the regression model free of endogeneity and enabling causal inference. The paper proves that the model is point-identified despite endogeneity due to omitted variables, that the proposed estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal, and that Jackknife resampling yields valid standard errors.

title: EXPRESS: The Role of Digital Ad Clutter in Ad Viewership and Memory
abstract: Advertisers face an increasingly cluttered digital ecosystem where customer attention matters. Despite this, the extent to which digital advertising clutter influences ad viewership remains unclear. This paper presents three separate eye-tracking experiments (subjects: N = 99, N = 250, and N = 575) using over a dozen custom-built web pages to better understand how digital ad clutter affects consumers’ viewing of digital ads. Across experiments, we show that increased clutter led consumers to allocate more attention to the overall advertising space and adjust how they distribute viewership across ad positions. A complementary survey revealed that clutter also reduced ad memory and recall for individual ads. We discuss the implications for advertisers and publishers regarding ad pricing and placement in crowded digital environments.

title: EXPRESS: Why are products so similar despite diverse consumer needs? The interplay between advertising and horizontal product differentiation
abstract: Firms are often less differentiated than standard price-competition models predict. We explain this gap by showing how firms can use informative or reminder advertising to soften competition. When firms choose locations, advertising, and prices endogenously, they may choose to soften price competition through limited advertising rather than greater product differentiation, allowing them to locate closer together while limiting price competition. This outcome of low advertising and central collocation is especially likely when advertising costs are high. We also observe that partially-differentiated equilibria, with one firm locating centrally and the other at an edge, and full differentiation, can each emerge under certain conditions. Thus, firms endogenously choose a mix of advertising and product differentiation to moderate price competition. Further, the shape of travel costs influences the equilibrium outcome. If the disutility from distance is highly convex, such as occurs when consumer preferences exhibit satisficing, central collocation becomes the unique equilibrium when more consumers are concentrated at the edge locations. However, when the disutility from distance is linear, having more customers located towards the edge locations makes collocation less likely. Overall, the interaction of advertising costs, consumer preferences, and location choices help explain why firms often forgo product differentiation.

title: The Emergence of the Service Techonomy: POPP at the Frontlines and the Rise of AI-Mediated Service Influence
abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence (AI), data infrastructures, and platform technologies are reshaping services and organizational frontlines. We conceptualize this shift as the emergence of the “service techonomy,” in which omni-personalization manifests via Prescribed, Omnipresent, and Personalized Persuasion (POPP; e.g., such that AI-driven agents guide frontline service interactions, determine service access and offers for consumers, and monitor and steer frontline employees). We derive four functional forms of POPP—interactive, pre-emptive, allocative, and governing—and organize them in a 2 × 2 matrix based on the timing of influence (reactive vs. proactive) and mode of influence (constraining vs. supportive). Anchored in evolutionary economics and the multi-level perspective on socio-technical transitions, our framework shifts attention from isolated technology and personalization features toward broader configurations of AI-mediated influence that shape service value creation, extraction, governance, and potentially inequality across customers, employees, and collectives in service ecosystems. This perspective provides a foundation for future theory building, measurement, and responsible design of AI-mediated services and organizational frontline research.

title: Music Marketing with Generative AI
abstract: The multibillion-dollar music industry faces severe content creation bottlenecks, making multimedia marketing assets prohibitively costly for smaller artists. This practice paper introduces a Marketing Asset Generation Engine (MAGE) that can produce over 700 million video ad variations reflecting each artist’s visual identity using only a music track’s audio and album cover as inputs. Collaborating with one of the world’s largest music labels, we conduct four preregistered field studies with over 11 million impressions across 75 campaigns for 33 music tracks on TikTok and Meta to validate MAGE. First, pooled across studies, MAGE-generated ads significantly outperform human-designed ads on TikTok with on average 26% higher click-through rates and 10% higher engagement, while we do not detect statistically significant performance differences on Meta, all at 98% lower production cost. Second, neither marketing professionals nor laypeople can reliably identify winning ads such that random sampling of MAGE’s outputs performs as well as human-curated selections. In contrast, an AI-in-the-loop system trained on past performance data can predict pre-launch which MAGE-generated ads will perform best for specific audience segments. These findings demonstrate that generative AI democratizes music marketing by making effective, on-brand video ads accessible at scale.

title: Service–Sales Ambidexterity as a Double-Edged Sword: Dual-Path Effects of Frontline Employee Appraisals on Performance
abstract: While prior research suggests that service–sales ambidexterity (SSA) can produce both beneficial and harmful consequences, why it results in positive or negative outcomes is less well understood. Drawing on the transactional theory of stress and job demands–resources theory, we propose and empirically validate a novel conceptual framework of frontline employee (FLE) SSA appraisal. Specifically, we explain how FLEs appraise SSA as a challenge and/or hindrance, and how these appraisals, in turn, influence their performance. A field study reveals that psychological climate shapes FLEs’ SSA appraisals: a promotion climate fosters challenge appraisals, boosting performance via work engagement, while a prevention climate drives hindrance appraisals, reducing performance via burnout. Furthermore, work meaningfulness of serving customers acts as a psychological resource that strengthens the positive effect of SSA challenge appraisal on work engagement and mitigates the detrimental impact of SSA hindrance appraisal on burnout. An experimental study complements the field study by demonstrating the causal effects of psychological climate on SSA appraisal tendencies. The findings contribute novel insights into the dual processes underlying SSA appraisal tendencies and provide actionable guidance for managers seeking to optimize FLE performance.

title: From Data to Decisions: Marketing Analytics, Mental Performance, and Firm Growth in an Emerging Market
abstract: Using a field experiment with 550 Rwandan firms, we show marketing analytics causally enhances entrepreneurs’ cognition and raises firm sales and profits.

title: Can Facebook Ads Prevent Malaria? Two Field Experiments in India
abstract: Two field experiments evaluate a nationwide Facebook malaria prevention campaign in India, finding effects concentrated in urban, more advantaged populations.

title: Exploitation in the marketplace: A consumer behavior perspective
abstract: Abstract This paper examines exploitation in the marketplace from a consumer behavior perspective. We define marketplace exploitation as occurring when one party leverages structural and/or situational resource asymmetries to extract disproportionate value in ways that undermine fairness or autonomy, even when exchanges appear voluntary and mutually beneficial. We distinguish marketplace exploitation from related concepts including fairness, deception, and discrimination, arguing that it centers on the morally problematic use of contextual advantage. Adopting a dual lens, we develop conceptual frameworks for both firm‐to‐consumer exploitation (e.g., price gouging, dark patterns) and consumer‐to‐firm exploitation (e.g., free trial abuse, exploiting firm mistakes). These frameworks delineate how structural and situational asymmetries give rise to objective exploitative acts, when such acts are perceived as exploitative, and how they shape emotional, cognitive, and behavioral responses. We synthesize a research agenda and outline methodological approaches for studying the antecedents, perceptions, and consequences of exploitation. This work contributes to consumer psychology by conceptualizing marketplace exploitation as both a subjective psychological experience and a strategic marketplace behavior, with implications for theory, policy, and ethical firm practices.

title: Collaborating on Research Transparency
Can green innovations enhance competitive advantage?
journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
abstract: Abstract Sustainable New Product Introductions (SNPIs) enable firms to meet consumers’ increasing demand for sustainable options while addressing rising expectations for corporate environmental responsibility. This study demonstrates that SNPIs can also strengthen brands by enhancing brand equity. Drawing on signaling theory, we propose that SNPIs serve as product-based sustainability signals that enhance brand equity by generating social goodwill. A staggered event study of the initial launch of a sustainable product line by a major laundry detergent brand shows that SNPIs can increase parent-brand equity. A complementary analysis of subsequent SNPIs across 15 leading brands in 12 retail chains reveals that this effect is moderated by parent firms' ethical reputation and retail chains' sustainable assortment share. These findings advance our understanding of whether and under what conditions sustainable products serve as credible signals of environmental responsibility and enhance brand equity.

title: EXPRESS: The Collecting Mindset: Viewing Purchasing as Collecting Enhances Acquisition Experience and Product Desirability
abstract: Abstract Managers often struggle to make acquisition processes engaging. While the dominant approach to reducing search costs has been to streamline the acquisition process, seven preregistered studies plus one supplemental study (N = 3,306) reveal an alternative pathway: Prompting consumers to view purchasing as “collecting” by positioning products as additions to their own collections, rather than as ad hoc purchases, improves consumers’ acquisition experience and increases product desirability. The authors demonstrate that activating such a collecting mindset shifts consumers’ psychological focus of the shopping process from securing a standalone product to instead investing in advancing their collection, thereby making them derive positive experience utility from the process, and in turn, elevating the desirability of the sought products. This research also offers practical guidance on how marketers can maximize the effectiveness of activating a collecting mindset: (i) encouraging active engagement in search, (ii) ensuring that search yields products that meaningfully advance the collection, and (iii) aligning the collection with an identity consumers value, as the effect may otherwise attenuate or reverse. These findings advance theory on everyday collecting and consumer search, and show how retailers and brands can strategically turn purchasing into a more positive acquisition experience that enhances product desirability.

title: EXPRESS: Lifestage Bias: How the Visual Representation of Product Lifespan Shapes Replacement Timing
abstract: To guide consumers’ decisions regarding when to replace products such as water filters, printer ink cartridges, and engine oil, companies often provide visualizations of the product’s lifespan. We document a lifestage bias in which representing a product’s lifespan with more (vs. fewer) visually distinct stages increases replacement intentions even when the product’s actual usage is the same. The effect emerges because a greater number of visually distinct stages leads consumers to mentally simulate previous use, thus enhancing the perception that a product has progressed through its lifespan and encouraging product replacement. Ten studies document lifestage bias and provide support (via mediation and moderation) for the underlying usage simulation mechanism. Notably, lifestage bias is eliminated when stages are represented non-visually or when stages are not visually distinct. Furthermore, lifestage bias is attenuated when product deterioration can be observed directly. These findings provide important insights into how consumers make product replacement timing decisions. Adjusting the number of distinct stages in product replacement guides offers firms and policymakers a practical tool to influence replacement timing—accelerating it when timely replacement is necessary for health, safety, or regulatory reasons (thus improving consumer welfare), or delaying it when items can be safely used for longer (thus reducing waste).

title: Coordinating the Frontlines: An Interdisciplinary Agenda for Extending Organizational Frontlines Research
abstract: Organizational frontlines research (OFR) has generated significant insights into the interactions between organizations and customers, the service interfaces through which these interactions occur, and how they unfold over time. However, less attention has been directed toward the mechanisms through which organizations coordinate these frontline dimensions. Building on Schneider and Bowen’s three-tier view of service organizations, we extend the OFR literature with a specific focus on the coordination tier, which consists of mechanisms responsible for integrating the boundary tier with the customer tier. Drawing on industry benchmarking survey data from senior service leaders and mapping these findings to established and emerging service research priorities, we identify six coordination-tier domains. These domains relate to the management of customer experience, service innovation, new technology exploration, service operations, culture and climate, and talent. By delineating key coordination challenges and a set of future research directions for each domain, we offer an integrated research agenda to advance interdisciplinary OFR scholarship. Additionally, we highlight the role of managers in coordinating resources and processes to deliver value across multiple touchpoints.

title: Populism and sustainable marketing practices: Insights from consumer-packaged goods manufacturers’ new product launches
journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
abstract: Abstract While sustainable marketing practices have traditionally been grounded in stakeholder capitalism, the rise of anti-climate-action populism presents new challenges to firms’ sustainable strategies. Drawing on resource dependence theory, this study argues that anti-climate-action populism prompts firms to reduce sustainable marketing practices, specifically the use of environmentally friendly packaging in new product launches. However, we propose that subnational formal and informal institutions, such as economic freedom and cultural tightness, attenuate this effect. To test these hypotheses, we employ a quasi-natural experimental design, using the announcement of the United States’ exit from the Paris Agreement to analyze its impact on sustainable marketing practices, based on a global sample of product launches by consumer-packaged goods manufacturers. Our difference-in-differences analysis supports these hypotheses. This study advances the understanding of the dynamic relationship between populism and subnational institutions, highlighting how different institutional pillars shape firms’ sustainable marketing strategies.

title: The Identification of the Dynamic Discrete-Choice Model with Stockpiling
abstract: We study the identification of the discount factor for dynamic discrete-choice (DDC) models of demand with stockpiling of a storable good. We show that the DDC has built-in exclusion restrictions that set-identify the discount factor without requiring any auxiliary assumptions. We compare this approach to previous work that assumes auxiliary structure on the storage cost function, clarifying how such structure generates exclusion restrictions and the corresponding data moments used for identification. Our key results show that these auxiliary restrictions are not necessary for identification; but that they are testable and can be included to achieve point identification and improve statistical efficiency. Using a case study of laundry detergent from earlier published work, we find a mean discount factor estimate of $0.957$, rejecting myopic models of choice in favor of the dynamic model. In counterfactual simulations, we show that some of the promotional lift during a discount period is indeed due to forward-buying. However, we predict considerably higher incremental sales compared to a standard discrete-choice model, which predicts that promotional discounts mainly cause substitution between brands. These results contribute to the long-standing discussion about the effectiveness of price promotions.

title: Platform-Based Servitization: Reconciling Competing Growth Logics for Industrial Firms
abstract: Servitization and platformization represent distinct logics through which industrial firms pursue growth. Servitization increases value through close customer integration, whereas platformization drives growth through ecosystem orchestration and scalability. These logics involve an inherent tension between relational depth and scalable flexibility, which the service literature has yet to resolve. This study draws on a systematic cross-field review of 129 articles spanning service, marketing, management, and information systems to theoretically ground platform-based servitization. We contribute to servitization by explaining how four configurational archetypes—product–service, customer solution, innovation, and transaction platforms—drive growth through platform-based servitization. Through a series of propositions, we explain how the cumulative layering of these configurations supports reinforcing and transformative pathways to growth, while data network effects emerge as a central growth mechanism, and combinatorial governance helps manage tensions between competing growth logics. We also contribute to platform scholarship by highlighting relational depth with customers and service partners as a critical condition shaping B2B platform transitions. For managers, our framework provides a strategic roadmap for leveraging platforms to move from digitalized product–service offerings to scalable platform growth. Finally, our findings open a research agenda for service scholars to further explore platform-based servitization.

title: From Live to Recording: Consumer Demand and Response to Price Across the Livestreaming Lifecycle
abstract: Using data from a knowledge-sharing platform that sells recorded versions of paid livestreams, this paper finds that demand is surprisingly more price sensitive before the event than after, which is explained partly by consumer self-selection and the lower quality uncertainty once the livestream ends.

title: The Aesthetic Paradox: How Visual Aesthetic Quality Shapes Digital Engagement on Social Media
abstract: Visual aesthetic quality (VAQ) is one of the most salient image characteristics of social media advertising, yet its nuanced effect on digital engagement remains underexplored. Building on existing research on the “beauty premium” and the “ugliness premium,” this research posits that the effect of VAQ follows a U-shaped pattern. Accordingly, a multi-study framework is proposed to verify both correlational and causal relationships. Study 1 quantifies VAQ of 11,559 post images leveraging the enhancer for aesthetics-oriented transformers (EAT) model, achieving an accuracy of 90.56%. Study 2 explores the correlation between VAQ and digital engagement via econometric analysis. Results reveal a U-shaped effect: both low and high VAQ lead to higher digital engagement than middle VAQ. This effect is more pronounced for posts with informational (vs. emotional) advertising appeals. Study 3 examines the causality with stimulus sampling and a randomized experiment, corroborating the findings of Study 2. Study 3 also uncovers the underlying mechanisms of the U-shaped effect: high VAQ enhances digital engagement primarily through perceived attractiveness, whereas low VAQ operates through perceived credibility. These findings refine the “beauty is always good” view into a nuanced U-shaped relationship and demonstrate how deep learning facilitates large-scale image analysis in social media.

title: Toward an Audience‐Based View of Incumbent Adoption of Potentially Discontinuous Technologies: Evidence From Fintech
abstract: ABSTRACT We advance an audience‐based view of incumbent adoption of potentially discontinuous technologies. Drawing on theories of discursive institutional processes and categorical legitimacy, we model how incumbents navigate mixed judgments from external groupings in their environment, that is, audiences, when adopting prospective discontinuous technologies. We argue that incumbents filter this noisy discursive environment by factoring in audiences' credibility and authority. We develop contextualized hypotheses and test them on a longitudinal sample of 149 incumbent financial firms responding to the emergence of financial technology in Europe from 2000 to 2016, distinguishing industry insiders, support experts, the general public, and regulators. Uniform engagement across audiences has a non‐linear influence on adoption. Incumbents respond most visibly to judgments from the general public and resist positive engagement from support experts. Industry insiders' and regulators' engagement did not have robust direct linear effects. Our findings reveal a preparadigmatic legitimacy puzzle wherein conventional institutional predictions systematically fail or reverse when legitimacy signals remain contested across audiences. We develop four propositions theorizing the expertise penalty, democratic legitimacy under uncertainty, authority without clarity, and temporal heterogeneity of audience influence, establishing the need to differentiate between audiences to understand incumbent responses in the preparadigmatic phase of technology evolution.

title: Business Model Bundles: Implications for Innovation in the Circular Economy
abstract: ABSTRACT Business model (BM) innovation is essential to the transition towards a circular economy, yet customers often resist circular BMs. This study investigates how manufacturers can innovate BMs for circularity in ways that increase customer acceptance. Drawing on a multiple‐case study of four manufacturers offering 21 product‐service system BMs, we introduce a new concept, the business model bundle: a strategic offering that packages multiple BMs within one contract and gives customers flexibility to move between them over time. We identify three defining characteristics: the combination of different BMs, contractual flexibility, and temporal transition. We theorize the BM bundle as a new form of BM innovation that creates, delivers, and captures value through the configuration of existing BMs rather than the invention of new ones. Our evidence indicates that the flexibility offered by BM bundles can reduce customers' initial commitment and make previously resisted circular BMs more acceptable. However, bundles may lead towards either greater or lesser circularity and therefore require deliberate design. The study extends innovation management and BM research by introducing the BM bundle that could open a new avenue in the field of BM innovation, and by identifying flexibility as a mechanism linking BM bundles to firm‐perceived customer acceptance.

title: Visual Plant Imagery and Property Valuation: A Descriptive Analysis
abstract: Online home profiles with more plant imagery are associated with higher property valuations, even after accounting for extensive property, neighborhood, listing, and market factors.

title: Signaling uniqueness: The psycholinguistic effect of language precision on product perceptions
abstract: Abstract This research reveals a psycholinguistic effect whereby more precise words in product communications increase consumer perceptions of product uniqueness. Drawing on Categorization Theory, the authors propose that more precise words in product descriptions are situated deeper within their semantic categories and denote narrower subsets of referents, thereby eliciting perceptions of product uniqueness. [Correction added on 15 October 2026, after first online publication: The reference in the preceding sentence has been removed.] Four experiments provide robust evidence supporting the “precise‐unique effect” and its underlying psycholinguistic mechanism driven by categorical depth. The findings further suggest that consumers' need for product uniqueness moderates the downstream effects of language precision on perceived attractiveness and behavioral intention via perceived uniqueness. This research contributes to the growing literature on language effects in consumer psychology and provides practical implications for making strategic lexical choices that enhance product positioning and differentiation.

title: Reconceptualizing Advertising Measurement in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming advertising by enabling large-scale creative automation, dynamic personalization, and AI-mediated consumer decision journeys. Existing measurement systems were developed for human-authored and relatively stable communication environments and do not capture how GenAI systems cocreate brand touchpoints with advertisers or mediate consumer evaluations of brands. In this study, we develop an integrated triadic framework for understanding the GenAI-mediated advertising landscape and reconceptualizes the action–mindset–behavior–finance measurement architecture to reflect an advertising process that is increasingly recursive, nonlinear, and adaptive. In doing so, we distinguish between traditional metrics that remain relevant but require reconceptualization and novel metrics unique to GenAI-assisted advertising systems. In addition, we extend the framework beyond firm-centered outcomes to incorporate stakeholder-oriented metrics relevant to employees, regulators, investors, and society. The framework offers guidance for scholars and managers seeking to evaluate GenAI advertising while maintaining transparency, trust, and competitive integrity. The study concludes with a future research agenda and crosscutting priorities addressing measurement, governance, accountability, and methodological challenges associated with GenAI-assisted advertising.

title: Advertising with HAART: Introducing Human–AI Asymmetric Relationship Theory
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)is rapidly reconfiguring advertising from message delivery and optimization to relationship-like exchanges between consumers and brands. While existing work has explained these interactions through social response accounts and interpersonal relationship theories, this lens risks overlooking a defining structural mismatch: AI agents convincingly enact relational characteristics but cannot experience relational benefits, costs, or commitment. Perceived mutuality can be high even when the underlying relational capacity for reciprocity is absent. We introduce human–AI asymmetric relationship theory (HAART), which conceptualizes AI-mediated relationships as relationally expressive yet structurally one-sided. HAART advances three tenets: (1) inherent AI agent characteristics limit relational reciprocity; (2) AI agents mask these limits through performative relationship actions, defined as linguistic, paralinguistic, and interactional behaviors that simulate relational engagement; and (3) when this masking succeeds, an asymmetric relationship emerges, characterized by asymmetries in dependence, risk, and control. We develop six propositions that detail the positive (e.g., enhanced support) and negative (e.g., heightened vulnerability) consequences for consumers and brands, and provide implications for theory, practice, and policy.

title: Symbolic promotions: Conceptualization and empirical investigation
journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
abstract: Abstract Symbolic promotions are an increasingly prevalent marketing practice globally, yet little is known about how or when they influence consumer behavior. We conceptualize symbolic promotions as a distinct type of sales promotion that creates value by reinforcing consumers' social identity through shared group membership rather than by providing economic incentives, such as reward-based promotions, or supporting distant others, such as cause-related marketing promotions (CMPs). We investigate the effectiveness of symbolic promotions and their underlying mechanisms using a multimethod approach. A nine-year longitudinal field study of daily sales for 22,084 books demonstrates that an existing symbolic promotion ("On August 12, I buy a Quebec book!") generates a substantial increase in sales, with stronger effects for lesser-known brands than for well-known brands. A follow-up experiment uncovers the unique mechanisms underlying these effects, showing that symbolic promotions stimulate curiosity and community rootedness, which in turn enhance multiple types of behavioral intentions, i.e., the likelihood of participating in the promotion, sharing it on social media, and future brand consideration. Together, these findings position symbolic promotions as a distinct, complementary addition to firms’ promotional portfolios, and demonstrate how firms can leverage shared identities to create value beyond traditional monetary incentives, with implications for various stakeholders.

title: Diagnosing image-ad success: An interpretable and scalable framework for liking, sharing, and memorability

title: How should companies use empathetic robots to drive consumer engagement, and under what conditions?
journal: International Journal of Research in Marketing
abstract: How does consumers' perception of robot empathy facilitate their engagement with robotic services? To address this question, we investigate the experiences of actual robot users across various service settings. Drawing on insights from exploratory interviews, a field survey, and a series of field and lab experiments with both Japanese robot users and international consumers, our research highlights how robot empathy can enhance consumer escapism and future usage across hedonic and utilitarian settings. Our findings further show that robot empathy facilitates consumer escapism and engagement in service environments characterized by low privacy sensitivity but may hinder these outcomes when privacy concerns are high. Managers should therefore implement emotionally resonant and imagination-triggering empathetic behaviors when privacy sensitivity is low, but dial down emotional expressiveness and instead focus on neutral support and professionalism when privacy sensitivity is high. This research contributes to the growing literature on human-robot service interactions by offering actionable guidelines for designing empathetic robots.

title: Do relationship disruptions increase spending on product categories high in eudaimonic value?
abstract: Relationship disruptions such as death of a spouse and divorce are among the most impactful events in someone’s life, yet current retailing literature does not document their influence on shopping behavior. In this research, we study the effect of relational disruptions on FMCG spending towards specific value orientations (utilitarian vs. hedonic vs. eudaimonic). Existing literature on eudaimonic consumption would predict that, since people derive meaning from their social connections, relational disruptions should increase spending for product categories that offer high eudaimonic value and hence deeper meaning. To explore this possibility, we apply difference-in-difference models combined with propensity score matching to a longitudinal dataset of U.S. households’ purchases across 998 product sub-categories. We find that households experiencing such negative life events increase spending modestly towards eudaimonic value and insignificantly towards other value orientations, offering important managerial implications for strategic category management. The effect is also attenuated when other family members are present in the household, suggesting a meaning restoration account.

title: Customer Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence (CAAI): Applications, Scale Development, and Testing
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming retailing, yet existing research on the extent to which individuals accept customer-facing AI-enabled retailing applications has largely relied on general technology acceptance frameworks and lacks a multidimensional, customer-centric measure tailored to retail AI contexts. Addressing this gap, the current research develops and validates a Customer Acceptance of Artificial Intelligence (CAAI) scale through a multi-study, multi-method program. The formative CAAI construct comprises eight first-order reflective dimensions: personalization, accuracy, safety, speed, convenience, humanization, friendliness, and emotionality. The 32-item full-scale and an 8-item condensed version are tested across diverse settings, demonstrating strong reliability, validity, generalizability, and predictive power. Moreover, the CAAI scale outperforms previously established measures relating to technology acceptance and artificial intelligence, providing a more precise and contextually relevant assessment of customer evaluations in retail settings. Results indicate that higher CAAI scores are associated with higher levels of word of mouth, share of usage, willingness to pay, and likelihood of adopting AI-enabled retailing applications. Thus, this paper provides a robust scale for assessing customer acceptance of AI and offers actionable guidance for both retailers and researchers.

title: AI product review summaries and content homogenization: the changing landscape of UGC

title: What if you dislike the brand you promote? How creatives' brand attitudes affect promotional content
journal: International Journal of Research in Marketing
abstract: This research investigates how creators' brand attitudes influence the promotional content they create for brands. It finds that professional creatives and other promotional content creators are more likely to use functional elements and less likely to include emotional elements when they have negative (vs. positive) brand attitudes. Importantly, the effect is driven by creators with negative brand attitudes: creators who dislike a brand seek to stay rational and suppress their emotions to reduce the perceived unwanted influence of their brand attitudes. Specifically, creators hold a lay belief that their negative attitudes might be detrimental to their work and that remaining rational and suppressing emotions are appropriate strategies to mitigate this concern. This, in turn, influences the functional and emotional elements included in promotional content. The effect cannot be explained by brand characteristics, specific grounds underlying creators' brand attitudes, or task difficulty.

title: Consumer scheduling of experiential activities in shopping centers
abstract: Consumers increasingly visit shopping centers, including shopping malls and city centers, to engage in experiential activities. Consequently, retailers and shopping center managers need to understand consumer visitation preferences for these activities and how they affect consumer store visits within a center. Existing consumer store location choice theory does not account for the experiential nature of shopping and ignores the role of experiential non-shopping activities in determining consumer store choices. To amend for this, the authors propose three ways in which consumer experiential activity choices differ from store choices as traditionally conceived. First, experiential activities tend to be discretionary, which means that consumers can choose to add more activities or end their visit at any time. Second, spending time on an experiential activity may represent a benefit instead of only a cost. Third, consumers may prefer to undertake experiential activities in particular, asymmetric orders. After outlining their theory, they present a formal approach to assessing the role of experiential characteristics of activities when consumers determine which stores and other activities in a shopping center to visit. An experiment in which participants schedule a visit to their city center illustrates and supports the role of experiential activities in determining consumers’ store choices. Follow up simulations explore how store choices would change when specific shopping or entertainment activities are added to the study area.

title: When format boundaries collapse: Price reactions of conventional retailers to national-brand listings at hard discounters
abstract: Hard discounters (HDs) have become a dominant force in grocery retailing, placing increasing competitive pressure on conventional retailers (CRs). As HDs expand their assortments to include more national brands (NBs), consumers can increasingly compare branded products across retail formats, weakening one of CRs’ traditional sources of differentiation. Yet little is known about how CRs adjust their NB prices in response to HDs’ NB listings, how these responses vary across brands and product categories, and how such price adjustments affect CRs’ sales. Drawing on data from over 300 NB listings by HDs across multiple product categories and three European grocery markets, we analyze pricing responses by leading HiLo retailers and the associated sales effects. We find that, on average, CRs lower NB prices after HDs list these brands. HD listings increase CRs’ NB sales on average, with price reductions further improving these sales outcomes. Although price reductions are larger for follower brands and lower-purchase-frequency categories, they generate stronger sales responses for market-leading brands and in more frequently purchased categories. Finally, among the observed price reductions, most do not improve short-run brand sales, whereas unchanged prices are rarely associated with declining sales that could have been mitigated through lower prices.

title: Customer air quality perceptions: conceptualization, scale development, and validation
abstract: Air quality affects how consumers experience retail environments. In their efforts to monitor and manage air quality, retailers often rely on objective measures. However, those measures do not capture consumer perceptions about their nuanced, lived experiences with the air. By developing a customer-perceived air quality measure for use in retail stores, the current research aims to help retailers understand and leverage these influential perceptions. Building on retail atmospherics and air quality research, as well as established scale development procedures, the authors develop and validate a scale with items pertaining to air breathability, circulation, freshness, humidity, scent, and temperature in Studies 1a–1e. Through content validity assessments, readability tests, and item judging, they establish a reduced item pool. Study 2 refines the scale to 26 items and provides initial validation with café customers; it shows that perceived air quality predicts dwell time, which predicts spending, whereas an objective air quality indicator predicts neither. Study 3 offers further validation among supermarket customers and supports customer-perceived air quality as a distinct perceptual layer of the retail atmosphere. Study 4 provides experimental validation. The resulting AirQual scale offers highly relevant implications for both theory and managerial practice.

From recommendation to revenue: Store-level evidence on the dynamic and spatial effects of the Net Promoter Score (NPS)
abstract: We investigate the effects of customers’ propensity to recommend a brand measured by the Net Promoter Score (NPS) on the sales of a publicly listed UK retail firm, which is dominant in the upholstered furniture market in which relatively expensive durable products have a long replacement cycle. From reasoning about word-of-mouth transmission, we theorize that store-level NPS effects are likely to (i) be nonlinear over time and (ii) depend not only on store’s own NPS but also on the firm’s neighboring stores’ NPS. We investigate the relationship between the NPS and sales over a 48-month period, matching every UK store’s monthly sales with its monthly NPS. We advance an econometric approach to allow for the identification of a non-linear time path. We find that the NPS, operationalized by surveying established customers six months after purchase, predicts future sales. Moreover, NPS sales effects unfold over many months along an “inverted U” time path: for own-store effects, from eight months after purchase, peaking at 10 months; and for neighboring-store effects, from six months after purchase, peaking at 11 months. Quantitatively, a sustained increase in the NPS across the company gives rise to substantial financial returns.
